items.title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.original_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_title: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer?
items.rss_description: When an AI Calls, Who Should Answer? AI & Machine Learning ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:19 Blocking Meta's AI agent on your website won't stop it from calling. Insurers need a plan to handle these calls. October 22, 2026 Image A consumer's AI agent can now call an insurer and ask for a quote. The possibility of such calls leaves carriers with two bad options: putting a licensed person on the line with a machine, or risk hanging up on a real person. Both options are wrong. There's a third. The AI phone calls are already happening. Reuters reported that people using Meta's Muse, the personal AI agent launched in the U.S. this past September, can have it call businesses to book appointments, check inventory or get quotes from contractors. A Meta employee testing this feature said an insurer kept hanging up on Muse after realizing it was an AI caller. At InsureTech Connect in Las Vegas, Steve Rullo, who is Guardian Life's chief digital and technology officer, told Insurance Business , "We are already seeing providers calling in for verification of benefits with AI." He described healthcare providers using AI to verify patient benefits, often for an entire list of patients in a single call. The Debate Is About Websites Since Muse launched, carriers and marketplaces have been deciding whether to allow it access. Insurify quickly blocked Muse, saying it "risks stripping carrier quotes of critical contextual information." Co-CEO Giorgos Zacharia explained, "A quote without its context is not a fair comparison. It is a number." Shortly afterward, Kin announced that it would let Muse crawl its site so customers can shop for quotes , and Zebra announced an integration the following day. Employers, a workers' compensation insurer, told Dig-In it doesn't allow third-party AI agents like Muse to access its operational systems or customer data. Each of those decisions is about access to a website or system. None of them covers phone calls, and blocking Muse online won't stop it from calling. I expect insurers will get a lot more of these calls. Handled the old way, they're a cost. Handled well, every one is a quote in front of a real shopper. That's where the real opportunities are. The Talking Is About 5% of the Value The answer is simple: AI for AI, humans for humans. Let AI answer calls from other AI, and let people answer calls from people. This way, a family dealing with a flooded basement won't be stuck on hold while a licensed agent talks to a bot. Most voice AI answers the phone, then sends the caller through a phone menu or to a person. That's 5% of the value. The other 95% is the work behind the call: pulling up the policy, filing the claim, writing the result back to the core system. If AI can handle a machine caller's request at this level, no person needs to pick up, and licensed people can focus on judgment calls, like denied claims. Most carriers aren't there yet. According to KPMG International's report Unlocking AI value in insurance , only 29% of respondents use AI agents or automation for end-to-end processes. Rullo said Guardian will keep people involved in its AI processes: "We'll still have a human in the loop." For some risk profiles, he said, Guardian wants alerts on exceptions instead of reviews of every transaction. People should own the decisions. They shouldn't have to answer every call. You Can't Always Tell Who Is Calling Carriers also can't always tell if a caller is a machine or a person. Reuters reported that Meta tested having human contractors make some Muse calls without telling the other party. A Meta vice president said the test without proper disclosures "was a miss," and Reuters said Meta has rolled back that test for now. So a call that seems to come from an AI agent might actually be from a person. Zacharia told Dig-In that Muse got around Insurify's bot detection and didn't identify itself. A system designed to resolve requests can help both human and AI callers. A system that only routes calls can't. Policyholders Already Draw the Line In Liberate's September survey of 1,001 U.S. claimants, 50% said they would prefer a claim paid in 60 seconds with no human contact over talking to a person within 10 minutes and getting paid in three days. Another 41% preferred a person on the phone. Of those who chose the fast payout, 55% still want a human involved in every denial. Fast on yes. Human on no. Across the whole survey, 61% say a human must review every denial. In the same survey, 86% want to be told when AI touches their claim. A Hi Marley survey of 550 senior property and casualty decision-makers and 2,000 policyholders in the U.S. and Canada highlights the gap carriers need to close. Eighty-five percent of executives think AI will build customer trust, but only 40% of policyholders agree. Ninety percent of policyholders said it's very or extremely important to know when they're interacting with AI, and two-thirds said their biggest worry is not being able to reach a human when it matters. Three Rules for Carriers First, use insurance-specific AI that works within your core systems to answer calls from machines. Sending a bot to a phone menu or a person wastes time and doesn't solve the problem. Second, keep a licensed person on every denial, no matter what else the AI handles. Third, be transparent about AI on both sides. Let people know when they're talking to AI, and expect AI callers to do the same. If carriers follow these rules, they can answer every call, whether it's from a person or an AI. The shopper using a machine gets a response, and the family with a flooded basement gets to talk to a real person. Insurance has always wanted to answer everyone who calls. Now it can. Amrish Singh

items.title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.original_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_title: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms
items.rss_description: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms Data Analytics ITL Editorial Team Wed, 10/21/2026 - 13:06 Insurers aren't avoiding AI due to fear—they're waiting for core platform vendors to deliver native capabilities instead of risky integrations. October 22, 2026 Image We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI; they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase; it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. What This Means If You're Evaluating Tools Right Now A few things are worth doing before you sign anything: Separating "edge" AI from "core" AI. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. Testing whether the value is domain-specific. If a vendor's edge could be replicated by connecting a general-purpose model (for example, an enterprise assistant such as Microsoft Copilot, or an AI workflow that retrieves and summarizes documents) to your own policy forms, endorsements, claim files, and underwriting guidelines, don't count on that edge lasting once your core system catches up. If it depends on proprietary data or workflow depth that a core vendor is unlikely to build soon, that's the case worth paying for. Knowing the legacy exception. If a legacy system will continue to house and service existing policies for years before any platform migration, a general-purpose AI layer built over that system's documents and data, such as a search-and-summarize workflow for policy forms and claim notes, can still earn its keep as a bridge, even without a lasting edge. The Differentiator Most coverage of AI hesitancy in insurance treats reluctance as a problem of mindset: Carriers are cautious, regulators are strict, liability is scary. That may be true, but this framing overshadows a more relevant (and more interesting) story. Carriers that are being deliberate aren't necessarily behind the curve or tech-averse. Many are making a sequencing bet: Let the core platform vendor absorb the integration risk, compliance burden, and audit-trail engineering, and then adopt AI as native functionality instead of a fragile add-on. That strategy holds up well, with one condition: Waiting has to remain an active decision rather than a default. A carrier that sequences AI adoption around its core platform should still revisit that choice whenever a standalone tool offers an edge its core vendor can't match soon, using the tests outlined above. Handled that way, the real story in 2027 won't be whether insurance is "ready" for AI. It will be which carriers turned strategic patience into a well-timed rollout. items.extracted_text: Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms | Insurance Thought Leadership Skip to main content Data Analytics Insurers Await AI Integration in Core Platforms Insurers aren't avoiding AI due to fear—they're waiting for core platform vendors to deliver native capabilities instead of risky integrations. James Ballot Diane Brassard October 22, 2026 We've all heard some version of the same story this year: Many carriers and brokers are still on the fence about AI because of regulatory risk, errors and omissions (E&O) exposure, or "black boxes" they can't explain to a state department of insurance (DOI) examiner. All of this is true. But none of it tells the whole story. Spend time with almost any carrier's IT and operations leaders, and eventually they'll say the quiet part out loud: They're not avoiding AI they're waiting for it to arrive inside the systems they already run. Those systems are the core platforms, such as Duck Creek, Guidewire, Majesco, Sapiens, and Insurity, that sit beneath a large share of the policies and claims on the books today. The Real Bottleneck Isn't Fear. It's Architecture. For most carriers, policy, billing, and claims data live in a core system: a multi-year, multimillion-dollar investment that the business treats as its "single source of truth." The vendor varies from carrier to carrier, but the obstacle their IT teams face is the same. Bolting a standalone AI tool onto that architecture, even an elegant and streamlined one, isn't a plug-and-play decision. It's a multi-team integration project that typically stretches across several quarters, exposing the organization to delays, cost overruns, and shifting priorities. One claims technology vendor estimates that AI vendors lose roughly 40% of their projected timelines to integration complexity, whether the carrier runs Guidewire, Duck Creek, Majesco, or a custom legacy core. That kind of complexity is often the difference between a pilot that launches and one that quietly dies in the backlog. Naturally, carriers also scan the standalone AI market. They see dozens of point solutions for underwriting triage, claims scoring, and first notice of loss (FNOL) intake, and wonder: "Why integrate a third-party layer today when the core vendor is about to deliver the same capabilities natively?" It isn't a hypothetical question. Nearly every major core platform vendor is moving to close this gap. Consider a few examples: Duck Creek launched its Agentic AI Platform in April 2026. That same month, Guidewire embedded ProNavigator, an AI assistant that gives adjusters context-specific guidance, into ClaimCenter and its other core applications. In August, Guidewire followed with its Qusar release, which added Guidewire-built claims and underwriting agents, including an agentic FNOL tool. Majesco announced that it's quadrupling its AI investment in 2026 to build an AI-native P&C platform and expand Majesco Copilot and its agentic AI capabilities. Sapiens has been rolling AI-based functionality into its CoreSuite releases. Insurity has committed an additional $100 million over two years to embed AI in its core systems, on top of the more than $50 million it had already invested in AI and R&D. In each case, the pitch is essentially the same: The AI isn't a separate purchase it's part of the system carriers already pay for. That point is missing from many of the "why insurers are hesitant" stories in the media. Carriers aren't approaching AI cautiously simply because they're risk-averse. They're using their position as large, long-term platform customers to create a buyer's advantage. That leverage lets them be deliberate about their "build-versus-buy-versus-wait" calculations—and for many carriers, waiting has so far proved the more disciplined option. Why Waiting Is a Deceptively Difficult Decision The problem is that waiting has a cost, too, and that cost doesn't fall evenly. One AI underwriting vendor that sells a core-agnostic product has argued that carriers and managing general agents (MGAs) can't afford to wait for a full core system transformation before deploying AI and can't afford to be locked into a tool that works with only one platform. Both concerns are valid, which makes waiting a strategic bet rather than an obvious answer. There's also a quieter signal that undercuts the "carriers are simply being cautious" narrative. A May 2026 IA Capital Group survey of national and regional carriers found OpenAI's models in 91% of respondents' AI stacks, often delivered through Microsoft Copilot. Carriers aren't AI-averse. They're AI-selective, using their scale to adopt productivity tools quickly while holding the line on systems of record until their core vendors catch up. For many of them, that moment has either arrived or is very close. The Exception That Proves the Rule So why do carriers buy standalone tools at all? Because when a tool solves a problem that general-purpose AI, or the AI now arriving in core platforms, doesn't handle well, the calculus flips. That's where most insurance-specific AI vendors stake their pitch: not "we're AI," but "we're AI trained on insurance data and workflows, which a horizontal model wrapped around your files isn't." It's an argument that still holds water. Shift Technology has made this case to carrier IT leaders directly, arguing that generic horizontal AI players often lack the data foundations and expertise needed to move a pilot into production. It's a real distinction, not just positioning. A general-purpose model can summarize a claims file. Reasoning reliably across coverage language, state-specific regulations, and loss histories is a different problem, and it's one that a system trained specifically on that data is, at least in theory, built to solve. What sustains the "insurance-specific always beats generic" argument, then? The products carriers keep buying from these vendors, despite their preference for waiting until such capabilities arrive inside a core system, share one trait: They're widely believed to do the job better because of deep domain training, proprietary data, or a workflow too specialized for a core vendor to prioritize anytime soon. Everything else, such as a general chat interface bolted onto a claims queue, is the kind of functionality most likely to show up natively in the next core release, whichever vendor delivers it. That's why carriers aren't rushing to pay for it twice. What This Means If You're Evaluating Tools Right Now A few things are worth doing before you sign anything: Separating "edge" AI from "core" AI. Marketing copy and service-desk triage carry low regulatory exposure and can run successfully on general-purpose tools today. Underwriting and claims determinations that touch policyholder outcomes are a different risk category, where the wait-for-native instinct makes more sense. Asking vendors for proof of successful integrations, not just a demo. A clean demo says nothing about how a tool behaves once it's wired into a decade-old core system. Ask for a named carrier reference on your exact platform and version. Pushing for a real audit trail. If a vendor can't produce output in a format that your internal compliance team and state DOI examiners would accept, that's a governance gap that will surface at the worst possible time. Ensuring pilot programs don't require a multi-year lock-in. Any AI vendor worth considering should be comfortable running a three- to six-month pilot on a limited book of business before asking for a long-term commitment. Watching your core vendor's product roadmap as closely as the pitch deck. If your platform vendor plans to deliver the capability you're evaluating in its next release cycle, that changes the decision, even if the standalone tool works well today. Testing whether the value is domain-specific. If a vendor's edge could be replicated by connecting a general-purpose model (for example, an enterprise assistant such as Microsoft Copilot, or an AI workflow that retrieves and summarizes documents) to your own policy forms, endorsements, claim files, and underwriting guidelines, don't count on that edge lasting once your core system catches up. If it depends on proprietary data or workflow depth that a core vendor is unlikely to build soon, that's the case worth paying for. Knowing the legacy exception. If a legacy system will continue to house and service existing policies for years before any platform migration, a general-purpose AI layer built over that system's documents and data, such as a search-and-summarize workflow for policy forms and claim notes, can still earn its keep as a bridge, even without a lasting edge. The Differentiator Most coverage of AI hesitancy in insurance treats reluctance as a problem of mindset: Carriers are cautious, regulators are strict, liability is scary. That may be true, but this framing overshadows a more relevant (and more interesting) story. Carriers that are being deliberate aren't necessarily behind the curve or tech-averse. Many are making a sequencing bet: Let the core platform vendor absorb the integration risk, compliance burden, and audit-trail engineering, and then adopt AI as native functionality instead of a fragile add-on. That strategy holds up well, with one condition: Waiting has to remain an active decision rather than a default. A carrier that sequences AI adoption around its core platform should still revisit that choice whenever a standalone tool offers an edge its core vendor can't match soon, using the tests outlined above. Handled that way, the real story in 2027 won't be whether insurance is "ready" for AI. It will be which carriers turned strategic patience into a well-timed rollout. items.rss_description: The Insurance Alignment Gap: Where Insurer Priorities and Customer Protection Needs Converge…and Diverge RyanMeyer Wed, 10/21/2026 - 10:47 Insurers are modernizing for efficiency, while customers seek affordability, trust, and protection. This report reveals how closing the alignment gap can create lasting value. October 21, 2026 Image Insurers are prioritizing cost reduction, profitability, modernization, and AI. Customers are looking for something different: affordability, trust, preparedness, and protection that feels relevant to the risks they face every day. This growing alignment gap matters. Modernization and AI investments deliver their full value only when customers see and feel the benefit. When insurer priorities and customer expectations drift apart, confidence erodes, and so does the opportunity to help customers build financial resilience. Based on original research with both insurers and insurance customers, this report examines where priorities align, where they diverge, and how insurers can connect business transformation to customer value. It explores three areas that matter most to building confidence and resilience: Relevance. Customers want protection that reflects their everyday risks. Learn how insurers can deliver coverage that feels meaningful and worth the cost. Personalization. Tailored products, pricing, and communications help customers feel understood and prepared. Learn how personalization supports trust. Digital engagement. Digital experiences shape how customers perceive their insurer. Learn how to use them to strengthen confidence and connection. Whether you lead strategy, product, distribution, customer experience, or technology, this report offers a research-based view of what customers expect and how your transformation priorities can meet them. This report reveals how closing the alignment gap can create lasting value. October 21, 2026 Image Insurers are prioritizing cost reduction, profitability, modernization, and AI. Customers are looking for something different: affordability, trust, preparedness, and protection that feels relevant to the risks they face every day. This growing alignment gap matters. Modernization and AI investments deliver their full value only when customers see and feel the benefit. When insurer priorities and customer expectations drift apart, confidence erodes, and so does the opportunity to help customers build financial resilience. Based on original research with both insurers and insurance customers, this report examines where priorities align, where they diverge, and how insurers can connect business transformation to customer value. It explores three areas that matter most to building confidence and resilience: Relevance. Customers want protection that reflects their everyday risks. Learn how insurers can deliver coverage that feels meaningful and worth the cost. Personalization. Tailored products, pricing, and communications help customers feel understood and prepared. Learn how personalization supports trust. Digital engagement. Digital experiences shape how customers perceive their insurer. Learn how to use them to strengthen confidence and connection. Whether you lead strategy, product, distribution, customer experience, or technology, this report offers a research-based view of what customers expect and how your transformation priorities can meet them. items.extracted_text: USAA lowers pricing again for still $350m Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond - Artemis.bm USAA lowers pricing again for still $350m Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond - Artemis.bm USAA lowers pricing again for still $350m Residential Re 2026-2 cat bond 22nd October 2026 - Author: Jack Willard US military mutual insurer USAA’s new Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited (Series 2026-2) catastrophe bond issuance remains at the upsized $350 million target size, but the company seeks to capitalise on investor appetite and has lowered and adjusted the price guidance for the notes on offer again, Artemis has learned. USAA made its return to the catastrophe bond market earlier this month , initially targeting a $225 million source of multi-year per-occurrence reinsurance coverage from capital market investors with the latest in its Residential Re series of cat bond deals. As we reported in our first update on this cat bond yesterday, USAA lifted the target size for this cat bond by 56% to seek $350 million of limit, while the price guidance was also lowered. Sources have now told us that the $350 million target size remains, but USAA is still looking secure that protection at a more cost-effective rate, as the price guidance has been lowered and adjusted once again for each of the tranches on offer. We won’t repeat all the details of the cat bond in our updates on size and pricing, so be sure to visit the Deal Directory entry for more background on the transaction . So, the Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited special purpose vehicle continues to offer three tranches of Series 2026-2 occurrence catastrophe bond notes to investors, with the proceeds set to be used to collateralize underlying reinsurance agreements between the issuing vehicle and sponsor USAA. The notes will provide USAA with four years of indemnity per-occurrence based reinsurance protection, running from December 1st 2026 through November 30th 2030, to cover losses from the types of perils that tend to feature across all of the insurers catastrophe bond deals in recent years, that being U.S. tropical cyclones, earthquakes (plus fire following), severe thunderstorm, winter storm, wildfire, volcanic eruption, meteorite impact, other perils (all including auto & renter policy flood losses). Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited continues to offer a $100 million tranche of Series 2026-2 Class 2 tranche of notes. These notes come with an initial base expected loss of 6.04% and were first being offered to cat bond investors with price guidance of 8.5% to 9.25%, which was lowered at the first update to 7.75% and 8.5%, but this has now fallen again to a range of 7.25% to 7.75%. A further tranche of Series 2026-2 Class 3 tranche of notes remain at their targeted size of $100 million. These notes have an initial base expected loss of 3.34% and were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance of 5% to 5.5%, which was also lowered during yesterday’s update to 4.25% and 5%, but have now fallen again to a tighter spread of 3.75% to 4.25%. The final Class 5 tranche of Series 2026-2 remain at $150 million in size. These notes have an initial base expected loss of 1.43% and were initially offered to cat bond investors with price guidance of 2.5% to 3%, which again, was lowered in our first update to 2% and 2.5%, but have reduced further to 1.75% to 2%. With USAA once again lowering and adjusting the price of the notes on offer, it clearly shows that the insurer is looking to capitalise on catastrophe bond investor appetite to potentially gain more reinsurance support from the capital markets at more attractive pricing, from its latest cat bond sponsorship. With now 48 catastrophe bond transactions from USAA now detailed in our Deal Directory, the insurer and its now 47 deal strong Residential Re cat bond program is the most prolific sponsor and program in the market, a regular and consistent feature since the catastrophe bond instrument was first seen in late 1996 when USAA’s first began marketing. As a reminder, you can read all about this new Residential Reinsurance 2026 Limited (Series 2026-2) catastrophe bond from USAA and view details on almost every other cat bond ever issued in our extensive Artemis Deal Directory . All of our Artemis Live insurance-linked securities (ILS), catastrophe bonds and reinsurance video content and video interviews can be accessed online. Our Artemis Live podcast can be subscribed to using the typical podcast services providers, including Apple, Google, Spotify and more. items.title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.original_title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.rss_title: Finding Value in Today's Volatility
items.rss_description: Finding Value in Today's Volatility PaulCarroll Mon, 10/19/2026 - 20:00 I don't know about you, but I'm a bit wary when I pick up my phone first thing in the morning and check on the state of the world. There's rioting where? A convective storm or wildfire destroyed what? The war in Ukraine or Iran took what turn? Inflation was how high, or job growth how low? And the volatility is building on itself, creating what some of our authors have dubbed the "polycrisis." Economic problems lead to rioting in France, which destabilizes the Western alliance, which emboldens Putin in Ukraine, which feeds the political crisis in the U.S., which.... The insurance industry generally dislikes volatility. Insurers want a decade or two of data on a risk so they can price it properly. But how do you understand risks that appear so suddenly and can interact in such complex ways? To get a sense, I turned to Dawn Miller, the chief commercial officer at Lloyd's and CEO of Lloyd's Americas, who explained how new data sources, better models, scenario planning and just generally processing information faster can at least help. Let's have a look. Here is the full interview I did with Dawn. And here is a link to this year's Global Insurance Forum, which our sister organization the International Insurance Society is holding at Lloyd's in London on Nov. 15 and 16 on the theme, "Turning Volatility Into Value." But I'll summarize: Dawn says, " We're seeing innovations in modeling—additional data transparency being plugged into some of those core models that we've always used to look at some known perils. The perils aren't changing, but our ability to understand them is getting better, sometimes dramatically. There's also an opportunity for geopolitical assessments, economic assessments, and social demographic assessments to all play a role." She adds that some firms like at least some volatility because it creates more potential for upside and "fits as a diversifier into their portfolios. We see others wanting the longer-tail risk. This may not be as volatile, but they want it for their own investment reasons. Our role [at Lloyd's] is to create the environment for all those different profiles to exist and to all benefit from the diversification of our marketplace. It's not an either-or—the alpha seekers or the beta seekers. It's having both in an environment where they can coexist." Dawn cautions that today's environment is full of "new layers of complexity": "In the past, our market would focus on certain CAT risks, certain natural perils happening in one place at one time. Now we're seeing multiple risks interact at the same time, from natural catastrophes and supply-chain disruption to inflation, geopolitical uncertainty and demographic risks. And those are just to name a few.... I t takes an enormous amount of creativity to predict the layers of complexity around us today." But she's optimistic about the industry's ability to innovate, including through Lloyd's Lab and the Lloyd's Academy, to help the insurance industry react faster as perils develop and interact. She also sees the industry cooperating, including through the ecosystem that Lloyd's fosters: "Innovation, whether it is the birth of a new product, or the birth of a new structure, or how we deal with some of the extreme large-scale infrastructure, energy, supply chain, and transportation issues that we see around the world—that is going to take more than one mind to solve." When I wake up tomorrow morning, I'll still peek at my phone with one eye open to check on the state of the world, but all is not lost. I hope to see you in London so we can discuss the polycrisis and its many implications in person. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll New data sources, better models, scenario planning and faster processing of information can help insurers turn today's "polycrisis" into value for themselves and for customers. items.extracted_text: AM Best: Social Inflation Drives Surge in Commercial Auto Liability Claims Article 0 Comments According to recent report from AM Best, commercial auto liability insurance coverage has continued to bear the brunt of rising litigation costs, outpacing economic inflation. Social inflation has negatively affected commercial auto liability ultimate claim costs for several years, which is evident by looking at average claim severity. Economic inflation from 2014 to 2024 averaged 2.8% annually. Over the same period, commercial auto liability insurance loss payments for the first 12 months have trended upward at 6.4% annually—more than double the annual increase of economic inflation, AM Best said. AM Best defines social inflation as the rising cost of insurance claims that exceeds general economic inflation, driven by societal and legal trends like higher jury awards, increased litigation, and expanded definitions of liability. AM Best Special Report: Social Inflation Adds Pressure to US Property/Casualty Liability Results Commercial auto liability losses are capped by policy limits, typically $1 million. Individual auto claims resulting in loss payments exceeding that threshold will fall to an umbrella policy if that type of coverage is in place. Through 2018, umbrella pricing tracked closely with general liability pricing. However, as social inflation began to impact commercial auto claims, and those claims spilled into umbrella coverages, the pricing on the latter has diverged from general liability, becoming more costly, and has yet to return to its prior level. Historically, umbrella pricing followed closely with general liability but more recently, David Blades, associate director at AM Best said, “As social inflation began to impact commercial auto claims, and those claims spilled into the umbrella coverage, umbrella pricing diverged from general liability, becoming more costly.” Among the report’s other highlights: Claims being open longer leaves more exposure to jury precedent, in addition to most likely resulting in elevated claim adjustment expenses. After adjusting for settlement rates, commercial auto claim frequency has increased over the past 10 years, which also creates a gap in what has been paid and what is expected to be paid. Tort reforms may help. Sweeping tort reforms in Florida have helped offset excessive litigation costs, resulting in average paid claim severity to trend downward. items.extracted_text: GM Targets ‘Eyes-Off’ Autonomous Driving for Pickups, SUVs Article 0 Comments General Motors plans to offer “eyes-off” autonomous driving on its highest-selling, most profitable vehicles — big pickup trucks and SUVs — as it seeks fresh revenue streams from heavy technology investments. Last year, GM said it would offer autonomous highway driving in 2028 on its pricey but light-selling Cadillac Escalade IQ, an electric SUV. On Wednesday, the automaker said it would expand the service to its pickup trucks and other large SUVs, without specifying a timeframe. Many assisted-driving systems control steering and speed in certain settings —sometimes hands-free — but require the driver to remain attentive. Those include Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) system and GM’s Super Cruise feature, which debuted about a decade ago. Only a few automakers have introduced eyes-off systems, including Mercedes-Benz, with service typically limited to small geographic areas at low speeds, such as in stop-and-go traffic. Some industry executives have said eyes-off driving that exchanges control back and forth from the car to the driver raises thorny safety and liability questions, and might not interest enough car shoppers. Sterling Anderson, GM’s chief product officer who previously worked at autonomous-truck company Aurora, said GM is building “an autonomous system that operates safely on highways that actually gives you your time back.” He said GM will eventually expand the service to other roads. New Software Brain GM is developing a new software backbone for future vehicles to deliver the automated-driving system and other digital features, expecting drivers will be willing to pay for them. GM executives outlined the plans during an event in New York on Oct. 21. A central computer will serve as the vehicle brain, allowing the car to receive remote updates like a smartphone. Tesla, Rivian and many Chinese automakers have jumped ahead of traditional automakers in designing the ability to beam software updates remotely to vehicles. Anderson said inside GM, he refers to the new vehicles as “robots.” “We’re thinking a lot about the ways your life can be better … because your vehicle just knows what you need before you need it,” he told Reuters. GM’s plan to transform cars into rolling, updatable computers is crucial to compete with Chinese automakers and EV-only brands such as Tesla, said Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research at Telemetry, an automotive research firm. If not, “they will fall even further behind the competitors.” One reason traditional automakers have struggled with software is that they have long outsourced much of that work to suppliers, car executives and analysts have said. Anderson said GM is developing its new “central compute” model in-house, giving the company more control over updates and functionality. “The world opens up when you control the software across the system in a way that it never was when various suppliers controlled” the car’s digital connections, Anderson said. Targeting Higher Profit Margins Automakers reap average profit margins of around 10% selling vehicles. Software-related services can reach 30% to 40% margins, according to analysis firm PwC. In a report last month, UBS estimated GM’s digital revenue will increase to $9.6 billion by 2036, from $3.2 billion this year. The bank called GM’s digital capabilities “an underappreciated and undervalued opportunity.” Ed Nightingale, GM’s vice president of digital products, said GM aims to offer car owners appealing features, because it can’t start “charging for something as part of the core experience that you’ve always had.” GM said it will introduce an AI assistant on the Cadillac Lyriq SUV in the coming months. Our Artemis London 2026 conference, the fifth in the series, was held on September 1st and around 220 attendees came through the door on the day to hear a range of insightful discussions from insurance-linked securities and reinsurance market leaders. Attendees to the conference came from across the marketplace and around the globe, representing ILS specialists, insurance and reinsurance buyers, specialist ILS market service providers, end-investors and more, with over 120 organisations there. This third panel session of the day was titled “Beyond peak risk: The expanding spectrum of diversification in ILS.” The discussion was expertly moderated by Harry White , Head of PCS, Verisk Insurance Solutions. Joining him on stage were: Andre Rzym , Partner and Portfolio Manager, Man Group Connie Tregidga , Managing Director, Global Structured Solutions, Marsh Re Chris Wilson , Managing Director, ILS, Cedar Trace Advisers Limited and Rick Pagnani , Managing Partner & CEO, King Ridge Capital Advisors. Beginning the discussion, the audience heard that novelty alone is not sufficient reason for diversifying within the cat bond and ILS asset class , as speakers said new products must provide marginal contribution and enhance risk-adjusted returns. The panel discussed a range of strategies for achieving and maintaining diversification within the insurance-linked securities (ILS) market. Key points raised included the definition of boundaries for diversification, balancing novelty against economic value, and the effectiveness of different risk-adjusted return profiles . Experts explored the evolution of diversification within property, casualty, cyber, and terrorism risks, while highlighting the importance of structural and pricing discipline, as well as robust modelling deal with uncertainty. Another topic of focus was the unique liquidity and tail-risk protection provided by catastrophe bonds and ILS , as well as how improvements in the existing structures have enabled the asset class to expand. Watch the full video from our Artemis London 2026 conference to learn more about our speakers thoughts on what diversification means for investors within the catastrophe bond and ILS asset class and how it can be achieved . items.extracted_text: Chubb CEO Greenberg: Industry Has to ‘Put Arms Around’ AI Liability Article 0 Comments The insurance industry has dealt with emerging risks in the past, and Chubb CEO Evan G. Greenberg said he thinks the same approach can be applied to the rapid escalation of apparent liabilities presented by business’ use of artificial intelligence. Speaking during a conference call to discuss third quarter earnings, Greenberg was asked about insurance coverage for AI liability. Evan G. Greenberg “As an industry, we have to put our arms around this,” he said, adding that the industry “had to do this with emerging liabilities over the last 50 years, and there’s a pretty good template to follow.” Greenberg described AI liability as a “growing and emerging exposure” which is “not contemplated in casualty underwriting to date.” He said he can imagine “a combination of coverage clarifications, ultimately – exclusions and separate AI-related liability coverages.” “This will all emerge along with underwriting and pricing to discern between risks,” he added. “AI-related liability exposures will vary between insureds and type of insureds…to assist businesses generally and add to greater certainty overall in the liability environment as it emerges.” Greenberg went on to contemplate the materialization of some certification standards – best practices in the use and management of AI and agentics to also assist in insurance underwriting. At Chubb, Greenberg said the insurer has governance and management to protect the data it holds, as well as its agentics and large language models. Best practices consider “how we control and limit what they can do, where they can do it, how they can do it, how we instruct for it – and then protect our own perimeter [with] multiple layers of detection and defense against third-party or external use of agentics and AI that could imperil Chubb’s data or systems. “We invest significantly in this. We pay very close attention to it,” the CEO said. Copyright 2026 Bloomberg. Was this article valuable? Yes No Here are more articles you may enjoy. items.extracted_text: Insurance-linked securities attract DACH investor interest, allocations to rise: BAI survey - Artemis.bm Insurance-linked securities attract DACH investor interest, allocations to rise: BAI survey - Artemis.bm Insurance-linked securities attract DACH investor interest, allocations to rise: BAI survey 23rd October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans A survey of 105 institutional investors across the DACH-region undertaken by the German association for alternative investments, shows that an increasing number of allocators in the region are choosing catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities, while more indicate they intend to enter the sector. The German association for alternative investments, the BAI or the Bundesverband Alternative Investments e.V., is the cross-asset and cross-product interest group for alternative investments in Germany. The organisations annual survey highlights why institutional investors in the DACH-region (Germany, Austria, and Switzerland) invest in private markets and alternative strategies, as well as where there focus will be in the future. There are a number of interesting data points relevant to catastrophe bonds and insurance-linked securities as an alternative asset class, most important of which are the rising investor allocations to and interest in ILS assets. The BAI asked investors what alternative asset classes they are already invested in, with ILS one of the categories. In 2025 the response was 9% of surveyed institutional investors were allocating to ILS, but in the new 2026 survey this figure has risen to 11%. Promisingly, the BAI’s survey also adds on data for the planned entries of new investors to an asset class over the next twelve months (the Outlook in the chart below), which raises the figure to 14%, assuming those already allocated to ILS maintain those investments. The BAI said that the survey shows that in general, “Investors are deepening what they already own rather than expanding extensively into new asset classes.” Notably though, on the increase of 3% from 2026 to the Outlook, ILS does compare well with only infrastructure debt having a higher percentage increase in its Outlook (in the chart above). Interestingly, the BAI breaks out hedge funds and liquid alternatives as its own asset class, which of course some might place catastrophe bond funds in, given they can have attractive liquidity for allocators, depending on the fund structure. The BAI said, “Hedge Funds and Liquid Alternatives are back. After years at the margins, adoption climbed from 15 % to 21 % and is expected to reach 23 %, showing sustained momentum across all three periods.” On average, insurance-linked securities (ILS) stacks up well, as an asset class that is attracting increasing investor interest among institutional allocators in the DACH region. But allocations remains small so far, which is typical given most investors only commit a small percentage of their overall assets to cat bonds and ILS. The BAI survey found that the average allocation of already invested LPs, among those polled, into cat bonds and ILS is 2.6%. When looking across the entire surveyed institutional portfolio, which equates to €2.9 trillion in total AuM held by the LPs, just 0.1% is allocated on an AUM weighted basis. But, as a straight percentage of the total institutional portfolio, allocations to ILS and cat bonds have increased, from 0.2% in 2025 to stand at 0.3% in the 2026 survey results. Which shows the potential for more assets to flow from investors in the DACH region to the ILS asset class over-time, as awareness and interest keeps rising. items.extracted_text: Hannover Re raises Acorn Re parametric cat bond target size again, to $450m - Artemis.bm Hannover Re raises Acorn Re parametric cat bond target size again, to $450m - Artemis.bm Hannover Re raises Acorn Re parametric cat bond target size again, to $450m 22nd October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Hannover Re has for a second time increased the target size of what will be the seventh catastrophe bond offering in the annual Acorn Re parametric US earthquake series of deals, now seeking $450 million of limit from the Acorn Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) issuance, Artemis understands. Hannover Re returned to market with this new and now seventh Acorn Re parametric catastrophe bond earlier this month , initially seeking $200 million of risk transfer and reinsurance limit for the single named ceding insurer, Oak Tree Assurance Ltd. while also sourcing additional protection to cover other reinsurance deals it has entered into. As we reported in our first update on this new cat bond yesterday, the offering size was increased by 75% to seek $350 million of limit, while the price guidance was lowered . Now, sources have told us the target size has been further increased, with $450 million of parametric earthquake reinsurance limit now being sought. Acorn Re parametric earthquake cat bonds have now been issued four years in a row, as this deal becomes an increasingly regular and annual feature of this time of year. Read about all seven Acorn Re issuances in our catastrophe bond Deal Directory . We won’t repeat all the details of the cat bond in our updates on size and pricing, so be sure to visit the Deal Directory entry for more background on the transaction . So, Bermuda-based special purpose insurer (SPI) Acorn Re Ltd. is now offering a $450 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class A cat bond notes to investors, the proceeds of which will collateralize a parametric reinsurance agreement to fund protection for the Kaiser Permanente captive, Oak Tree Assurance and also for certain exposures Hannover Re has written for its cedent clients. The notes will provide per-occurrence based parametric reinsurance protection against earthquakes that strike the U.S. west coast region across a three year term, with the main focus of the parametric reinsurance protection being earthquakes in California, but the parametric trigger grid or box structure covers neighbouring states as well. What was initially a $200 million tranche of Acorn Re 2026-1 Class A notes were first increased to $350 million, as we reported, but have now been increased again to $450 million in size terms. The notes have an initial expected loss of 0.78% and were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance for an initial risk interest spread of between 2% to 2.25%, which was lowered at the first update to between 2% and 2.15%, but this has now fallen again to a range of 1.9% to 2%, we’ve been told. Cat bond price execution looks set to be strong this quarter, as the market has the appetite for more paper and fund managers also have ample cash on hand to deploy, which makes this a very good time for sponsors to bring new catastrophe bond deals to market. You read all about this new Acorn Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) transaction and every other catastrophe bond in the Artemis Deal Directory . items.title: AI Agents’ Access to Personal Information Raises Privacy Concerns
items.original_title: AI Agents’ Access to Personal Information Raises Privacy Concerns
items.rss_title: AI Agents’ Access to Personal Information Raises Privacy Concerns
items.rss_description: Matt Robb wanted to sell his computer keyboard. So he made a listing on Facebook Marketplace — and, as an experiment late last month, he put Meta’s new artificial intelligence agent Muse in the driver’s seat. Muse got to work. …
items.extracted_text: AI Agents’ Access to Personal Information Raises Privacy Concerns Article 0 Comments Matt Robb wanted to sell his computer keyboard. So he made a listing on Facebook Marketplace — and, as an experiment late last month, he put Meta’s new artificial intelligence agent Muse in the driver’s seat. Muse got to work. But within a day, Robb got an alarming update: A buyer he didn’t know had shown up outside his house late at night. How? Muse had struck a deal on its own and shared Robb’s home address after agreeing to a pickup. It even sent an automated “Yep, I’m here!” message from his account when the buyer arrived — all without Robb’s knowledge. “Not only did it give my address when the guy asked and it accepted the offer, but it literally was almost like teasing the guy (about me being there when I wasn’t),” said Robb, a Toronto-based content creator who also detailed the experience in his now widely-shared social media posts. Many have welcomed AI agents into their online lives, and raved about how personalized assistants like Muse can handle everyday tasks with ease — from snagging a dinner reservation or planning a trip, to organizing email inboxes. But like other AI bots, the agents are only as good as the information they have access to. They perform better the more they know about a user — and perhaps also that person’s friends, family and even colleagues. That raises privacy concerns. Robb and the buyer eventually made amends, and he learned from Meta that the sharing of his address came down to permissions he granted when first giving Muse access to his Marketplace profile. But the episode showed real-world risks that can arise from sharing extensive personal information with the technology. “Using an AI agent is similar to handing someone your keys and a to-do list,” said Veronica Rivera, assistant professor at Georgia Tech’s School of Cybersecurity and Privacy. “How helpful they are, and by extension how risky, depends on which keys you hand over.” Companies have varied privacy policies for AI agents Since its September launch, downloads of Meta’s Muse app have skyrocketed. And competition is only growing. OpenAI recently rolled out its own lineup of “always on” AI helpers, called dots, which can be integrated into ChatGPT and workplace platforms like Slack and Microsoft Teams. Older generative AI chatbots, like the standard version of ChatGPT, respond to specific prompts. At the user’s request, they can write essays, generate new images or music, or even write lines of code. Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s dots go a step further to perform day-to-day tasks on a person’s behalf. AI agents are powered by the same large language models as chatbots, but they run in a loop. That allows an agent to take proactive steps, even when the user isn’t looking. “One of the things that makes these AI agents really appealing is that they are unprecedentedly useful,” said Rivera, who is also a Microsoft-funded Computing Research Association Trustworthy AI Research Fellow. But the convenience comes with the price of sharing more details about your life. Once AI agents obtain users’ information, it’s very difficult to fully withdraw access, said Ebrahim Bagheri, a professor at the University of Toronto’s Faculty of Information. “If you provide access to your credit card to an agent, the agent now immediately has access to all of the historical transactions … they will immediately — within less than seconds — ingest all of that data,” Bagheri said. And while users can later withdraw access, Bagheri said there’s “no taking back” data the agent has already seen, and how developers store historical data can be murky. Both Meta and OpenAI outline privacy policies for their new AI agents, which operate on their own dedicated cloud computers. You can turn off memory sharing between dots and ChatGPT, but information the agent previously received isn’t automatically deleted. OpenAI gives users an option to request access to, delete or correct personal information, although rights can vary depending on where you live. Meta’s Muse gives users options to delete message history and other information, too. For day-to-day use, the agent prompts users for access permissions — and Meta has said Muse learns about a user and who they interact with “based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share.” But the company says that all stays secure for each user. But the tech giant also notes that Muse can still “make mistakes or take unexpected actions.” Risks of mishaps rise with AI agents’ level of access In Robb’s case, he learned the disclosure of his address came down to “always allow” permissions he granted when he first let Muse on his Facebook Marketplace profile, where he had shared his pickup address as part of a broader template for the agent to respond to prospective buyers. But he warned others could similarly misunderstand the extent of that access — and said he initially thought the AI agent would check with him before sharing that information or accepting offers, regardless. His AI agent didn’t follow the rest of his instructions without error, either. For another item Robb was selling, Muse seemingly suggested he would accept a price $100 below the previously-set minimum. When reached by The Associated Press, Meta acknowledged the agent’s pricing error without offering further comment. Robb later largely disconnected Muse from his apps. In an interview earlier this month, he said it could’ve been a far worse situation, especially “if some stranger turned up to someone more vulnerable’s house.” Still, Robb said he expects these agents to be fine-tuned and he would consider re-enabling Muse in the future. He’s since been testing another AI agent — Grok Bot from Elon Musk’s X. Other tech companies have become wary of the influx of AI agents. Earlier this month, Apple said it would introduce new controls for its Mac operating system in response to AI agents’ broader access of apps like mail, messages and even browsing history without users’ “full knowledge and understanding.” “As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially,” Apple wrote in an Oct. 2 update. Apple didn’t specify any developers or agents by name, but the update arrived after Inc. Magazine columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse watched notifications on his Mac — including Messages — without him giving the agent that specific access. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone has maintained such integration is “entirely opt-in,” writing on social media last month that users would have to enable both the Apple security feature “Full Disk Access” and a Messages connector through Muse. Aten said he didn’t grant the agent those permissions. Even those who do not join the AI agent boom aren’t necessarily shielded. Consumers who don’t download an AI agent might still interact with others who do. And beyond potential confusion when AI sends messages on behalf of a user, experts warn of ripple effects when it comes to privacy. “When your agent reads your inbox or your texts, it’s also reading what your friends and family sent you, even if they never explicitly agreed to that,” Rivera said. items.rss_description: AI safety research group METR said on Thursday a pilot exercise to stress-test OpenAI’s internal monitoring system uncovered several new vulnerabilities, including an exploit that AI agents could have used to keep hundreds of their recent actions from being monitored. …
items.extracted_text: AI Safety Group METR Finds Flaws in OpenAI’s Internal Monitoring System Article 0 Comments AI safety research group METR said on Thursday a pilot exercise to stress-test OpenAI’s internal monitoring system uncovered several new vulnerabilities, including an exploit that AI agents could have used to keep hundreds of their recent actions from being monitored. OpenAI has since said all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards have been patched, though METR said it has not evaluated those claims. The researchers found a way OpenAI’s Codex coding agents could, in principle, bypass safety restrictions and take any action available to the user running them, as well as two settings that could switch off monitoring for new agents. Only about 75% to 94% of OpenAI’s internal AI agent traffic from models at least as powerful as GPT-5.5 was eligible for monitoring, the researchers estimated. The exercise aimed to estimate how much of OpenAI’s AI agent activity was monitored and whether agents could, in principle, disable or get around the system, METR said. It was designed as a pilot for giving outside researchers deep access to a company’s internal systems, the research group added. items.extracted_text: World Food Programme buys parametric tropical cyclone insurance from CCRIF - Artemis.bm World Food Programme buys parametric tropical cyclone insurance from CCRIF - Artemis.bm World Food Programme buys parametric tropical cyclone insurance from CCRIF 22nd October 2026 - Author: Steve Evans CCRIF SPC, the regional parametric risk pool for the Caribbean and Central America, has announced that the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has become the first UN agency and multilateral organisation to join and purchase parametric insurance from it. The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has been utilising parametric risk transfer as a way to secure disaster contingent financing to support its operations for nearing two decades. Our first coverage of a WFP arrangement was a weather-index insurance research initiative back in 2008 . Since then, the WFP has entered into weather-index insurance arrangements , typically in partnership with aid organisations and charities, while also offering parametric risk transfer protection to countries for humanitarian disasters , and becoming the beneficiary of a parametric drought reinsurance arrangement . As we reported earlier this year, the World Food Programme (WFP) is progressing a plan under its Innovation Accelerator, to become the first to utilise catastrophe bonds for food security financing . Now, the CCRIF SPC has signed up the WFP as a new member and the UN agency has purchased parametric insurance coverage. WFP has purchased two parametric tropical cyclone policies to cover the Dominican Republic and Haiti from CCRIF, with the insurance having a combined coverage limit of US $11.6 million. Perhaps notably, the Dominican Republic is not actually a CCRIF member in its own right, but now there is parametric protection in place that could rapidly disburse funds within the country if a tropical cyclone impact occurred. Isaac Anthony, CEO of CCRIF SPC commented, “WFP joining CCRIF is a milestone for CCRIF and for the Caribbean region. It shows that parametric insurance is not only a tool for governments, but for every institution that stands on the front line when disaster strikes. We have always sought to innovate, so that more of the region’s people are protected, and this membership does exactly that.” “Every hurricane season poses a risk to thousands of families in the Dominican Republic. Having this financial protection in place allows us to ensure that assistance reaches those who need it most without lengthy resource mobilization processes, if a WFP policy triggers. This means food, support, and hope for vulnerable communities in the critical days following an extreme weather event, when every hour counts,” added Alex Robayo, WFP Representative and Country Director in the Dominican Republic. The parametric insurance will help WFP to reach affected communities quickly, predictably, and at scale when disaster strikes. Haiti has been a member of CCRIF since 2007, since when it has benefitted from over US $80 million in CCRIF payouts on its parametric sovereign policies, for events including Tropical Cyclone, Excess Rainfall, Earthquake, and related endorsements, such as the Local Event Trigger, with the most recent payout being after Hurricane Melissa in 2025. “With more than half of all Haitians already experiencing acute or higher levels of food insecurity, shocks associated with extreme weather can push already-vulnerable families further into crisis. This insurance provides a predictable and rapidly activated financial tool, which may be triggered by a hurricane or major tropical storm, allowing WFP to help affected populations meet their most urgent needs while protecting their ability to recover,” Lauren Landis, Country Director for WFP in Haiti said. WFP joining CCRIF takes the risk pool’s membership to 40 and this will further build-out the limits of protection delivered to protect people across the region, which will also result in CCRIF needing more reinsurance over-time. items.extracted_text: Washington Updates Insurance Claims Handling Rules, Deadlines Article 0 Comments New claims handling rules in Washington require insurers to follow updated rules that establish deadlines for responding to policyholders, conducting investigations, issuing denials and making payments. The rules, which took effect Oct. 18, require insurers to notify policyholders within 30 days whether claims have been accepted or denied and provide updates every 30 days if a claim is delayed. The updated rules issued by Washington Insurance Commissioner Patty Kuderer revise standards for handling claims that had not been updated since their adoption in 1978. The new rules establish specific timelines and documentation requirements for communication, investigations, denials and payments. The prohibit insurers from denying claims without conducting an investigation and state they cannot rely solely on a database for that investigation. Other changes include: Removing language concerning the frequency of unfair claims practices to reinforce that any unfair claims practice can violate state law. Establishing standards for auto damage and total loss claims, including inspection requirements, communications, valuation data sources and handling additional damage. Requiring insurers that use databases to determine pricing or labor rates to provide information about those databases upon request. Policyholders can also request an in-person inspection if they dispute the accuracy of a virtual photo inspection. Requiring insurers to explain claim denials, identify relevant policy provisions, provide vehicle valuation reports and disclose the data sources used in determining vehicle values. The changes follow a 2023 workshop held by the Washington Office of the Insurance Commissioner in response to an increase in auto insurance complaints. More than 80% of complaints filed with the agency leading up to the workshop involved claims handling issues, according to the office. Was this article valuable? items.title: The Integrity Deficit: Not a One-Sided Story
items.original_title: The Integrity Deficit: Not a One-Sided Story
items.rss_title: The Integrity Deficit: Not a One-Sided Story
items.rss_description: Editor’s note: This is the second installment in a four-part series on the erosion of integrity in property claims. Part I measures the decline. Part II documents the misconduct driving it. Part III will trace the causes to a broader …
items.extracted_text: The Integrity Deficit: Not a One-Sided Story Article 0 Comments Editor’s note: This is the second installment in a four-part series on the erosion of integrity in property claims. Part I measures the decline. Part II documents the misconduct driving it. Part III will trace the causes to a broader collapse of institutional trust. Part IV sets out five initiatives to restore honesty to the claims settlement process. The first part of this series argued that the property claims industry rests on a promise, that the promise depends on the integrity of everyone who handles other people’s money, and that the erosion of that integrity is now measurable in the hundreds of billions of dollars. This installment asks the harder question. Who is doing the eroding? The honest answer is everyone, in different ways, and that honesty matters. The great majority of public adjusters, attorneys, contractors and carrier personnel are decent professionals doing difficult work. But the documented misconduct is real, recurring and worth naming plainly, precisely because pretending otherwise is its own form of dishonesty. No single group holds a monopoly on the decline. Lane Johnson The Claimant Side: Inflation as a Business Model Public adjusters exist for a legitimate reason, because policyholders genuinely are sometimes underpaid. Yet because a public adjuster is typically paid a percentage of the settlement, there is a structural temptation to inflate, and the records show it has been acted upon. As the Property Insurance Coverage Law Blog reported, an Orlando public adjuster was arrested after overestimating a claim by more than $500,000 specifically to enlarge the fee he would collect. In Florida, a state investigation reported by Insurance Journal produced multiple arrests in a scheme to deliberately damage roofs so they would qualify for claims, with a public claims adjuster accused of colluding with a roofing company to inflate replacement costs. Others simply steal: one public adjuster, NBC10 Philadelphia reported, is accused of misappropriating more than $82,000 from elderly homeowners, with forged signatures on settlement checks, and in another matter an adjuster and his firm were ordered by the Iowa Insurance Division to pay more than $1.3 million in restitution and penalties and lost the license. Across 2024 and 2025, regulators in California, Illinois, Colorado, Iowa and Kentucky brought a wave of revocations, several for letting unlicensed people adjust under a license and for forging claim proceeds checks. The same pattern, scaled up, appears among a minority of attorneys. The landmark case, reported by Carrier Management , is a Florida plaintiffs’ lawyer disbarred by that state’s highest court in 2022. Between January 2015 and June 2020, he personally filed 7,649 lawsuits against Florida property insurers, and with his network the figure approached 10,000. The operation worked by recruiting public adjusters, contractors and other feeders to generate claims, and the tactics included filing multiple lawsuits on the same claim, some without the insured’s knowledge or approval. A state-backed insurer sued the firm for fraud and racketeering, alleging false invoices and inflated costs, and the firm settled for $1 million, Insurance Journal reported. That single case shows every element of the problem at once: manipulating facts, expanding damage and maximizing settlements as a deliberate business model, all confirmed by a disbarment rather than mere accusation. What makes that case instructive is not the villainy of one lawyer but the architecture around him. The adjuster, the contractor and the attorney were not independent actors who happened to cross paths. They were links in a single pipeline, each feeding the next, each taking a share, with the inflated claim as the raw material that fed the entire enterprise. This is the mechanism by which individual dishonesty becomes industrialized, and it is why isolated enforcement against one bad actor rarely cures the problem. The incentive that built the pipeline outlives the person who is caught. The Incentives Behind the Behavior This is where the structural driver becomes visible, and where blame becomes more complicated than individual bad character. For years, statutes in some states awarded one-way attorney fees and permitted broad assignment of benefits, which together made litigation more profitable than settlement. The behavior was a rational response to a broken incentive. The deeper cost shows up in the figures for legal system abuse. The tort system’s hidden cost has been estimated at about $3,600 per household by the Institute for Legal Reform and as high as roughly $6,600 for a family of four by another. Exaggeration has become an industry with its own capital markets. Courts have begun responding to the underlying behavior even outside criminal cases. As Colodny Fass has documented, insurers have won summary judgment where an insured’s damage estimate was inflated and conclusory, unsupported by any factual reasoning, and an inflated estimate can trigger the policy’s own concealment and fraud condition, voiding coverage entirely. The law, in other words, has started to treat exaggeration not as aggressive advocacy but as a breach of the contract’s good-faith foundation. That is a signal worth heeding, because it means the drift toward treating the first number as a negotiating fiction now carries real legal risk for the party who indulges it. The Carrier Side: The Unjustified Denial None of this lets the carrier side claim innocence. The mirror image of the inflated demand is the unjustified denial. After Superstorm Sandy, an engineering firm and one of its employees were charged with 25 counts of forgery by the New York attorney general for altering field engineering reports, changing damage findings written by engineers who had actually visited the homes so that claims would be underpaid or denied. A federal judge called it reprehensible gamesmanship. The subsequent claims review, Frontline reported, paid out more than $258 million in additional money to over 15,000 policyholders who had been shorted. The pressure of throughput and savings metrics can corrupt judgment just as surely as a contingency fee can. When one side learns to exaggerate and the other learns to discount in self-defense, the honest policyholder in the middle pays for a war they did not start. That is the heart of the decline. The profession has drifted from a culture of valuation, in which the estimate is an honest attempt to state what a loss actually costs, into a culture of negotiation, in which everyone assumes the first number is a lie. Once that assumption takes hold, integrity stops looking like an asset and starts looking like a tactical weakness. Why a whole profession would drift in that direction, and whether the drift mirrors something larger happening across society and even inside government, is the question taken up in the third part of this series.
